title: Agency Growth Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures how well your fundamentals, AI operations, hiring culture, and growth stack are aligned to scale without shortcuts.

questions.text: How clearly defined is your unique positioning in your market?

answers.label: We offer essentially the same services as other agencies in our space
We have some differentiation but it is not sharp or ownable
We have a clear niche but have not built real moats around it
We have strong positioning backed by specific case study results
We have a defensible position that competitors copy but cannot replicate

questions.text: How much of your new business comes from relationships and referrals versus cold outbound or paid acquisition?

answers.label: Almost all new business comes from cold outbound or paid channels
Occasional referrals, but we depend on paid or outbound to fill the pipeline
Roughly half comes from relationships, half from cold channels
Relationships are our primary pipeline source with cold channels as backup
Relationships and reputation fill our pipeline without paid or cold outbound

questions.text: When results dip or growth stalls, what is your first move?

answers.label: We add a new channel or test a trending tactic
We change the creative or adjust the offer quickly
We review the data and tweak current tactics
We audit the fundamentals — offer, messaging, audience — before touching any tactic
We always run a full diagnostic on fundamentals first, with data, before any channel change

low.headline: Your fundamentals need a real audit before anything else.
low.text: You're trying to scale on a shaky foundation. The two moats that actually matter are relationships and unique positioning. If competitors can screenshot your work and copy it pixel for pixel, you have not built either. Start there before adding any new channels or tools.
steps: Write one sharp sentence describing who you serve, what you do, and why you're different — then test it against your three best clients and see if they'd agree
Track your last 10 new clients and find how each one came in. If less than 30% came from a relationship or referral, you do not have a relationship moat yet
This quarter: every time results dip, make yourself audit the offer and messaging before touching any channel

mid.headline: You have a foundation — now make it defensible.
mid.text: You know what you stand for, but your positioning is not moated yet. Most agencies at this stage have a niche on paper but have not built the case study proof or relationship depth to own it. Fix that before you scale spend.
steps: Take your best 3 case studies and rewrite each as a specific outcome story: before and after numbers with a time window attached
Run a relationship audit — reach out to every past client and warm prospect this month and track who responds. That is your relationship capital
Pick one positioning claim you want to own and run all content and outreach around it for 90 days without shifting it

high.headline: Solid. Now protect what competitors cannot screenshot.
high.text: You've got positioning and relationships working. The risk at this stage is complacency — letting shortcuts creep into your creative or operations because things are going well. That is when the cracks show up.
steps: Document what makes your client relationships sticky and build a system to replicate that experience for every new client
Review your positioning quarterly against what competitors are copying — if they're lifting your branding, update your creative before they close the gap
Make the fundamentals audit part of your quarterly leadership review, not just a tool you reach for when things dip

questions.text: How systematically does your team use AI and automation for internal operations?

answers.label: A few people use AI tools individually with no shared system or process
We have some AI tools set up but no shared process or team training
We have automated a few tasks but it is ad hoc and undocumented
We have identified key workflows and automated them with training and documentation
We run a self-hosted automation stack with documented, trained, and maintained workflows

questions.text: When evaluating AI tools or agents for your business, how do you make the call?

answers.label: We adopt what is popular or what our peers are already using
We try one tool and stick with it unless it clearly fails
We test two or three tools side by side occasionally
We run structured tests with defined success metrics before committing
We run ongoing, unbiased benchmarks across tools and switch when the data supports it

questions.text: How do you use AI in your creative and content production?

answers.label: AI generates most of our ads, scripts, and content with minimal human edits
We rely heavily on AI UGC and generated creative for speed and cost savings
AI generates drafts; a human reviews and approves before anything goes out
AI speeds up ideation and variation; humans make all final creative decisions
AI is one part of our creative variation — it accelerates testing but never replaces quality

questions.text: On average, how many hours per week does each team member spend on tasks that could realistically be automated?
questions.hint: Think recurring reporting, data entry, client follow-ups, and manual admin. Most teams underestimate this — be honest.

questions.text: How many team members regularly perform these manual tasks?
questions.hint: Count everyone who spends meaningful time each week on work that should be automated.

questions.text: What is the average fully-loaded hourly cost for these team members?
questions.hint: Fully-loaded means salary + benefits + overhead. Quick estimate: divide annual fully-loaded comp by 2,000 working hours.

low.headline: AI is costing you money right now — just not in the way you think.
low.text: You're either not using AI, or you're using it in ways that create real risk. AI-generated creative with no human review and no disclosure is a liability, not an advantage. The real opportunity is internal: find the 3 most time-consuming tasks your team does every week and automate those first.
steps: List 3 tasks your team repeats every week that follow a predictable pattern — those are your first automation targets
Set up your own n8n instance and have a dev or devops build the first automation, then train the team on it before building the next one
Stop using AI UGC or generated testimonials without disclosure — as regulations expand past New York, the legal exposure outweighs any CPL savings
Test at least two AI tools for any given workflow before committing — stay unbiased and let the data decide, not what is trending

mid.headline: You're using AI, but you're not building infrastructure.
mid.text: Ad hoc automation is better than nothing, but it breaks under scale and creates knowledge silos. The agencies doubling this year have a documented, trained automation stack — not a collection of one-off shortcuts held together by whoever built them.
steps: Document every automation you have built: what goes in, what comes out, who owns it, and what to do when it breaks
Run a real benchmark between your current AI tools and at least one alternative — do not assume your current setup is optimal
Find the one automation saving the most hours and make it bulletproof before building new ones on top of it

high.headline: You're using AI the right way. Now track what it's actually worth.
high.text: You're treating AI as a force multiplier, not a shortcut. That is the right frame. At this stage the job is to quantify what your stack is saving and use that data to make better investment decisions — not just assume it is working because you built it.
steps: Track time saved per automation quarterly and report it to leadership — this data shapes where you build next
Stay unbiased on tooling. What performs best today may fall behind in 3 months — keep running benchmarks
Audit your AI creative use annually for compliance risk as disclosure laws expand beyond New York

questions.text: When a team member hits a difficult problem or makes a mistake, what is your typical response as a leader?

answers.label: I step in, fix it myself, and explain what went wrong
I tell them exactly what to do next time
I explain the right approach and have them execute it
I ask questions to guide them toward the answer
I consistently ask 'What would you do?' and let them own the solution

questions.text: What is your primary filter when making a new hire?

answers.label: Credentials and technical skills are the main filter
Portfolio quality and past results drive most decisions
A mix of technical skills and rough culture fit
We weight attitude and care for clients as heavily as technical ability
We hire on gut and heart — whether this person truly cares about the work and the clients

questions.text: How involved are your executives or founders in day-to-day client relationships?

answers.label: Executives are the main client contact on most accounts
Senior staff lead but executives join most client calls
Account managers handle day-to-day; executives join monthly or for escalations
The team owns client relationships and escalates to execs when genuinely needed
The team leads everything; executives are backstops, not front-line contacts

low.headline: Your leadership model is slowing the team down.
low.text: If you're the smartest person in every room, you've built a ceiling. The smartest-person-in-the-room hire is not the one who stays — the one who cares about the client and the work is. And if executives are on every client call, the team never develops the confidence to run without you.
steps: This week: every time a team member asks you a question, respond with 'What do you think?' before giving your own answer. Do it for 30 days straight
Audit your last 3 hires — what actually predicted performance? Credentials or attitude? Use that to rewrite your next job description
Pick one account where an executive is the main contact and transition full ownership to a team member within 60 days

mid.headline: Your team is developing — but execs are still in the way more than they need to be.
mid.text: You're hiring for attitude and giving the team room to grow, but the instinct to step in is still strong. That instinct costs the team more than it saves you. The goal is a team that runs client relationships so well you're proud to be out of them.
steps: Remove yourself from at least two recurring client calls this quarter — hand them fully to a team member with no safety net attached
Create a simple internal escalation rule: what does a team member have to try before they bring a problem to leadership?
Review the hire from the past year who surprised you most positively — what stood out at the interview? Build that into your next candidate scoring

high.headline: Strong culture. Protect it as you scale.
high.text: You've figured out that caring beats credentials and that the team runs best when execs get out of the way. The risk now is that hiring speed at scale erodes what you have built. Keep gut and heart as your primary screen — not just a tiebreaker when the scores are close.
steps: Document your hiring philosophy so it survives beyond you — write down what 'caring about clients' actually looks like in a first interview
As the team grows, build a way for senior team members to develop others on client relationships, not just technical skills
Revisit your escalation process every 6 months as team size changes — what worked at 10 people tends to break at 30

questions.text: How coordinated are your paid media, SEO, creative, and retention efforts in terms of shared strategy and data?

answers.label: Each channel runs independently with its own goals and reporting
Channels share some data but strategy decisions happen in silos
We have shared dashboards but each channel still runs its own strategy
Channels are aligned on shared KPIs and a common performance roadmap
Acquisition, retention, creative, and measurement run as one integrated growth system

questions.text: When evaluating a new ad platform or channel, how do you make the investment decision?

answers.label: We follow what is trending or what competitors appear to be testing
We test based on vendor pitches or peer recommendations
We run small tests but decisions are mostly intuition-based
We test with clear hypotheses and defined pass/fail metrics before committing budget
We test rigorously, compare intent quality vs. CPL, and make fully data-led platform decisions

questions.text: How quickly does your team act on campaign performance insights?

answers.label: Insights sit in reports that rarely drive actual changes
We review monthly and adjust quarterly
We review weekly but changes take 1-2 weeks to get into market
We review weekly and can act within a few days
We have systems that surface insights and allow same-week iteration on creative or targeting

low.headline: You're running channels, not a growth system.
low.text: Siloed channels mean siloed data, which means slow decisions and CPLs that are higher than they need to be. I have seen brands cut media spend by 30% just by aligning paid and retention data into one view. That is not a technology problem — it is a coordination problem.
steps: Get all channel owners together this week and map every metric each tracks. Find the 3 that all channels share and start reporting those together
Before your next channel test, write down what success looks like before you spend a dollar
Set a 7-day review cadence for your top campaign and track how long it takes your team to actually act on what you find

mid.headline: Shared dashboards are not the same as a shared strategy.
mid.text: You have data alignment but strategic alignment is still missing. A shared dashboard that each channel ignores in its own planning is well-organized overhead. The goal is one growth roadmap — not four channel plans that happen to live in the same doc.
steps: Create a single performance roadmap with one owner, one set of priorities, reviewed weekly by all channel leads
Before your next channel test, write a one-paragraph hypothesis: what you are testing, why you expect it to work, and what the pass/fail threshold is
Find the insight from last quarter that took the longest to act on — trace why, and remove that blocker

high.headline: You're running a real growth system. Now cut the time from insight to market.
high.text: Integrated strategy and fast iteration are the right combination. At this stage, every day between an insight identified and a change live in market is a day of wasted spend. That gap is where the right automation layer earns its cost.
steps: Map every step between an insight identified and a change live in market — find the single biggest time bottleneck and address it first
Review your channel mix quarterly against intent quality, not just volume — high-volume, low-intent traffic is a growth trap
Keep running unbiased channel tests even when the current stack is performing — what works at your current scale may not work at the next

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
